utterances.text: A Muslim will be the President of the government, the Prime Minister. We have got a very excellent man Fikret Abdic. We have already agreed with Fikret Abdic. He will be the Prime Minister and the Serb will be the President, and the Muslims will be satisfied and all those that remain in Banja Luka as well.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain -- you hear about this plan first from the soldier or from Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that if I remember correctly, I think that I first heard it from Kuprasanin and shortly thereafter from the soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges who is Mr. Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Prior to the war, he was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, he left the Presidency and established paramilitary formations that cooperated with the military formations of the Serbs and Croats -- cooperate with Martic's police and later on with the Serb forces and they jointly attacked the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got very much more for this witness, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to just tie this up, this encounter with Mr. Kupresanin and perhaps another few questions. Not very much at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Five past two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.28 p.m. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, before we paused for the lunch break, you were testifying about Mr. Fikret Abdic. Who was Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that he was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, elected after the first free multiparty elections. At first he was a member of the Party of Democratic Action, and later on, he left it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was a member of the Presidency, was he a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the executive board of the SDA at any time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is possible that he was in the beginning, but I am not sure of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, he was a candidate for President of the State in the election of 1990, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he was a candidate for the membership of the Presidency of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, his name was on the ballot, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of Mr. Izetbegovic was on the same ballot, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that on that election, Mr. Abdic won the most votes, the majority votes?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he received more votes than Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to state that Mr. Fikret Abdic is a Muslim, Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified and stated that he, relating to Mr. Abdic, later attacked army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that the --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- army of Mr. Izetbegovic's Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the pull-out of the Yugoslav People's Army from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established. On exactly what date it was established, I do not know that, but I know that the Territorial Defence was established in early April, and after that, it grew into the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Abdic separated from the government which was headed by Mr. Izetbegovic and declared his own entity in north-western Bosnia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. A part of the area in which he was present, he split off and he declared an autonomous province there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you name a few bigger towns in that region?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that area, Bihac, Velika Kladusa, Cazin Buzin, Bosanska Krupa that is the area of the Bosnian Krajina, and in the area in which Fikret Abdic proclaimed autonomy was Velika Kladusa and a portion of the Cazin municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you testified that Mr. Abdic later attacked the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that means you basically stated there was an arms conflict between two Muslim armies?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There existed a defence formation of Bosnian army in Bosnian Krajina, at one point Fikret Abdic who at that time was in the territory of the Republic of Croatia issued directives and returned to Velika Kladusa and split off that area with the assistance -- with the weapons which he received from the Bosnian Serbs, he was able to corral that territory and I don't know more about that territory because I was not in that territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you know from the press reports at that time, could you inform the Court when was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that Mr. Abdic and his followers, the autonomous region that he declared as separate from the central Muslim government in Bosnia, cooperated with the Serbian entity known as Autonomous Region of Krajina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I could read that in the media, and also see it on television and other mass media. At the time when he did this, he was no longer a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He stepped down from that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the followers and members of his insurgent troops were majority Muslims, were they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Members were, for the most part, Muslims, but the officers for the most part were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you are testifying before this high court today is that Muslims from Bihac area, Sasinska Krajina so called as you testified earlier, had indeed very close cooperation and military alliance with Serbs from Autonomous Region of Krajina, including Prijedor, that you are from?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have been talking about the impressions which are gained from reading reports in the press and watching things on television, so I was talking about what I saw something regarding Velika Kladusa and not Buzim and Sasinska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any military actions between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, under central authority of Mr. Izetbegovic, and troops, formations loyal to Mr. Abdic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The army units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were under the control of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not Alija Izetbegovic because he was only one member of this Presidency, were defending the country and the aggressor's forces were attacking it. Apart from the Serbian aggressors, there was also the militia of Fikret Abdic which was engaged in this aggression. This is what I knew from the general mass media, and I did not have any personal additional knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question, Your Honours, along this line. Mr. Semenovic, do you know whether there were any prisoners of war taken between two Muslim armed groups, armies, armies of Mr. Izetbegovic and military formations of Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Tadic's trial, you testified that Mr. Kupresanin had informed you that the Serbian entity in Bosnia is about to form a coalition government with Mr. Abdic whereas Mr. Abdic was supposed to be the President of the new political entity. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember it, but the interpretation is wrong. Kupresanin was talking that the President of this entity, of this Serbian state, was going to be a Serb, and Abdic was going to be the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the position that you were considered for was a member of the parliament of such an entity. You testified to that effect, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not told this by Kupresanin, I repeat, I was told this by a soldier who drove me from the municipality building back to Vrbanja, and I did not have a conversation with him. He just on his own commented that "It was good that you decided to become a member of the Serbian assembly." And several days later, Kupresanin came and said that they would probably take me to Knin and from Knin, we would probably go to Bihac, to the demarcation line with UNPROFOR because we were going to start negotiations there. However, he told me nothing about the nature of my presence there. I just know that I was terribly afraid of this possibility and I refused it even at the cost of my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time, you looked Mr. Kupresanin straight in the eyes and said "I can't go to Knin, I can't go to Knin or these negotiations," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not dare say it in that way. I told him, "Sir, Mr. Kupresanin," this is as far as I recall, "I don't know how much this will contribute to these negotiations, but I believe that it will not be of much use. However, you are a smart man. You know these things best. So you decide." In other words, I was trying to be conciliatory. I did not want to tell him openly that I wasn't going to go because I knew where I was, nor did I tell him that I did not want to go. After this conversation he said, "We'll still come for you tomorrow and we'll take you there on a helicopter, maybe even a car, because I don't like flying in a helicopter." And in these following days, I expected to be taken -- to be picked up by the police and taken there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, in fact, you never made that trip, did you? You were not forced to go.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they did not take me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were waiting for a possible trip to negotiate with the Muslim representatives of Mr. Abdic, you were recuperating at your sister's home in a suburb of Banja Luka, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the contents of the conversation of Kupresanin and the military officers who came and who talked to my sister. They said that I needed to put on some weight and recover, and in those days, they kept bringing food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, do you recall whether any of the Serb authorities, soldiers, ever brought you any food as they promised?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, once -- I don't know the exact date when this was -- but they came to Vrbanja, that is Kupresanin did and some officers, and they brought a lunch package. There was some cooking oil and beans and some other food items in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more point here in your contacts with Mr. Kupresanin. Mr. Kupresanin picked you up in his limousine and drove you to Banja Luka; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was a car -- this was an official car of the Banja Luka municipality, of the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Tadic's trial you testified that you had casual conversation with Mr. Kupresanin upon entering the car, and then it seems there is an hour gap, and then you arrived at your sister's home. What, if anything, has Mr. Kupresanin told you during that limousine drive from Omarska to Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have a casual conversation, I was answering the questions which he was asking me, and I listened to what he had to say. During this trip, the driver stopped at one point and picked up two soldiers who were hitchhiking, and for the most part of the trip, they talked to the soldiers about the front-line in Gradacac, in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mention to the Court -- what is Gradacac, where is it located, and why was Mr. Kupresanin interested in military situation in Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During the trip from Omarska to Banja Luka, there was a bus stop about ten kilometres out of Omarska and two soldiers were standing there hitchhiking. Mr. Kupresanin told the driver to stop and pick them up, and he asked them where they were on the front. One said that he was at Gradacac and the other one as I recall said that he was on the front-line at Jajce. Then he asked them what the situation was like where they were, how many days of holiday they got and those were basically the contents of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just asked you a simple question and if you can answer with a very short answers. Your Honour, I ask for some latitude here. Who was fighting whom at the positions in Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The soldiers said that they were fighting Ustasha, those were the words that they used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Gradacac is located east from Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, Gradacac is on the border with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how many kilometres approximately east of Banja Luka is Gradacac located?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you care to state that the Gradacac's military activities were part of the battle for corridor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that on the radio, that there was fighting for the corridor, but we didn't know anything, we were under siege, so what I could -- the only information I could get was from the radio and maybe from the Croatian media, so I could only sort of guess what was going on. I did not know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have testified that you and the citizens of Kozarac were blocked at some time at the beginning of May of 1992. Do you know for general information whether the whole region of Krajina was blocked from the eastern part of Bosnia because of the closure of the corridor along the river Sava by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not know that at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn that fact, Mr. Semenovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard it on the radio, in the following days, that there was fighting for the corridor. There was fighting against the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and on the other side, the other side was the army of the Serbian Bosnian army, that is of this new state which the Serbs had established and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Do you recall when did electrical power was disconnected to Kozarac and Prijedor in April or May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that there was -- that the electrical power was cut off in Prijedor. Maybe there were shortages, maybe there were interruptions, but I know that immediately before the attack on Kozarac, the power was cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But to the best of your recollection, Trnopolje had electrical power until the very day when you were forced to leave the city or the village, is that correct, or perhaps there is another explanation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct. All Serbian households in Trnopolje in the village had an uninterrupted supply of electrical power throughout the fighting period because we could see the lights on, whereas in the Muslim areas, including Trnopolje and Kozarac, there was no electrical power at all. In one area in the Krajina area -- in these Ukrainian households they also had supplies, but for the most part, all the way to the foothills of Mount Kozara, the electrical power was cut off from most households.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a mining engineer. Perhaps just as having general engineering background you might know the answer to the following question: Where was the electricity supplied to Prijedor and Banja Luka? Where from? Only if you do know.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that exactly, not exactly. I suppose that part of the electricity came from the mid section of Bosnia and the other from somewhere else, I'm not sure from where, what quantities, and where they came from. It's really not -- doesn't have much to do with my profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified in Tadic's trial that you overheard two conversations between Mr. Kupresanin and Dr. Radovan Karadzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that you definitely recognised the voice of Mr. Karadzic having heard him speak on the floor of the parliament and also, I believe, in some personal contacts; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I rarely had personal contact, maybe on two or three occasions when I had, on behalf of the club of SDA members of the parliament, take over to them some bills, and occasionally in that club, Mr. Karadzic would be present as well. Those were very rare contacts, maybe just on two or three occasions, and those were formal -- the contacts were of a formal nature. And, of course, his voice, I knew his voice very well, because Mr. Karadzic was a frequent speaker at the parliament when the members of SDS were present at the Bosnian parliament. I managed to recognise the voice, not on the first occasion when Mr. Kupresanin talked to him from Omarska but on the second occasion in Banja Luka in the municipality building, since I wasn't far away from the telephone and I could hear. Usually when you have old telephones, you can hear that -- I heard a voice similar to Karadzic's and the content of the conversation convinced me later on that indeed it was Dr. Karadzic on the other line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the first conversation, besides Mr. Kupresanin and yourself, who else was present in those two rooms, as you testified?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the room where I was, I was brought in by a policeman, and when Mr. Kupresanin came in, the policeman left and I remained alone with Mr. Kupresanin and then we started a conversation, as I have indicated before. And then from a nearby office, they called him and they said that the president needs to speak to him on the phone, and he got up and went to answer the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see any other persons being present in the other office?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think there was a person or somebody, there were some official persons there, but this is what I could see from the hallway and through the other doors that were diagonally across. I couldn't even turn back. This is just what I could see without really moving my body, just using my eyes, because indeed I was in a camp where there were terrible conditions, and you had to be aware of every millimetre of your movement and your behaviour, and at one point, when he was talking, carrying a conversation there, Mr. Merkic entered the room and he wanted to start a conversation with me but I didn't dare really start a conversation, and after a while he left, and from the other office, the only thing that I heard was about the beds and the soaps and the sheets. I heard it twice. It was repeated twice. He said, "I found only one of them." I didn't understand the essence of it. It was only clear to me later on when he told me that I needed to go with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you observed Mr. Kupresanin speaking with Dr. Karadzic, did you hear these words: "Blankets, beds, detergent" directly from the telephone in Dr. Karadzic's voice or perhaps you heard Mr. Kupresanin repeat them?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear what was said on the other side, I heard what Kupresanin said. He repeated those words, that he needed soaps, detergents, 300 beds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you heard Mr. Kupresanin convey those requests or orders to anybody at that time or at any time later on in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear him talking about those orders to somebody else, I heard him carry on a similar conversation on the phone in Banja Luka, but he wasn't issuing orders. He wasn't ordering somebody to bring that in, he was just mentioning the same things again, and he also mentioned clothes for me, a job, as far as I could remember he was saying, "All right, all right." He was confirming some of the statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are testifying now that it was Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic who requested a suit and good treatment for you because you overheard him directly, in Banja Luka it wasn't Kupresanin repeating, it was Karadzic's voice that you could overhear from the old-fashioned telephone on the desk?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Based on what I had heard, I repeated several times what I had heard, I concluded that it was ordered to Kupresanin to go to Omarska and search for the surviving members of the parliament and put them somewhere where they could get better and then use them for his political purposes. This is how I understood the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what you have just testified that you understood, that is not what Dr. Karadzic said. What I asked you only, what did you hear in his own voice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One minor point. Mr. Semenovic, I will direct your attention to the very first day when you surrendered yourself to the authorities of the detention centre in Trnopolje. What was the name of the captain that you were turned into?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: His name was Slavko and I heard that from Adem Trnjanin a friend of mine who later went on to this Slavko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Trnjanin make any comments who to turn into and not to turn into?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He asked me to surrender because he was afraid that they would kill 15 persons, including himself, because they were given the ultimatum with a deadline of 48 hours, and he told me that Slavko would not beat me, he was solely interested in how I entered Trnopolje camp and how I exited the camp. This is what Slavko wanted to hear from me. This is what Adem told me, and he didn't say anything about the others, and he was beyond himself. He could barely speak about that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wouldn't be fair to conclude that the inmates, refugees, at Trnopolje centre, had favourable opinion about Captain Slavko?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Captain Slavko was interrogating some of the 15 persons that I have mentioned. Among others, he also interrogated Adem Trnjanin, and at the end of that interrogation and abuse, some of them were beaten. They issued the ultimatum. What else was said in the conversation, I do not know, but Adem said he will not beat you, he's only interested in how you entered the camp, because Slavko was the head of the guards at the camp, and he was only interested in how I was able to enter the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Captain Slavko was almost your neighbour before the war started, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, I had not known him. It is possible that he was my neighbour but maybe further away from my house. I really didn't know him. I didn't recognise him when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were then taken to the -- or the car that you were driven in stopped in front of Keraterm factory and you testified you observed the prisoners in that camp in very, very poor shape, and you observed a building across the street. Who was housed at that time in that building?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The car stopped across from the Keraterm camp, and on the road, going on the road from Trnopolje towards Prijedor, we, in front of Prijedor, came to the point where this road connects with the road Prijedor-Banja Luka, and at that spot, on the right-hand side is the factory, Keraterm, and the property that belongs to it, that's next to the road, and on the left side are some kind of buildings that belong to one of the companies from Prijedor, so the car stopped on the other side across from Keraterm in the back yard, right through the gate, and in that building was the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe any uniformed men in and around Keraterm factory?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Behind the car through the right window, so next to the soldier and in front, I saw the fence of the factory property, and I saw a large number of people, inmates, inside the camp, and I couldn't see the other part of the factory property. I could see a large number of uniformed persons leaving the building that I have mentioned, the building in front of which the car had stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any uniformed men on the other side of the road, on the Keraterm side?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I could see a smaller portion of the factory property, the fence, and also a large number of inmates along the fence, and then further inside, the portion that I could see, I couldn't see the whole Keraterm and the whole factory property and I couldn't see what was going on on the other side of the property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In comparing Trnopolje and the building in Trnopolje and comparing the building of Keraterm, just the physical structure, Keraterm building is indeed very, very close to the road, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it's close to the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any machine gun nests at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't notice it from the car, the area to 30 to 40 metres around the car, I couldn't see any machine gun nests, there was just a very high fence, and along that fence, I saw those people, but I repeat to you that I could see only a portion of that area through the window of the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I apologise to the Court and also through the Court to the witness that I am asking for these details. I know it's very difficult for him. But I will just move on with this as quickly as possible, Your Honour, because I know that it's very painful for him to go through these things. Mr. Semenovic, just one minor detail. Once you were put into the cell in the police building, in the police, basically, prison, cells, in Prijedor, you testified about the horrible situation of the cells, the condition of other people, but at one point you stated that the -- somebody knocked on the door and you were supposed to clean a dorm. Who were the people who knocked on the door and whose dorm were you supposed to clean up?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Special police. And the person that knocked with his foot on the door, that hit -- and who was verbally abusing me was Dragan Saponja who beat me the previous day in the SUP building just prior to the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is indeed so reprehensive and I deeply feel for your suffering. However, in your testimony you mentioned that you were woken up and you were supposed to clean up a dorm. Whose dorm were you supposed to clean up?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the dorm of the special police that slept there, the special police. When I was taken into the cell, when I was taken into the first door, I was beaten right in front of the cell door. Several of those soldiers beat me. And the next door of the next cell was open, and I saw the beds in there, and I saw that it was a dorm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise to you, Mr. Semenovic, but I was under the impression, and I checked it in the transcript, I believe that you mentioned yesterday that was military police. That's why I was confused. I just wanted to find out was that police special units of the ordinary police of the police that we know belonged to --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it wasn't an ordinary police, it was special police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But based on the uniforms, was it special police in blue uniforms, as is the traditional colour of the police in Yugoslavia, or is that military police?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. It wasn't a civilian police, it was a special police. Yesterday, when giving the answers to some of the questions, I explained the difference between the uniforms that they had and the rest of the uniforms. I said that they had sort of a purplish uniform, it was also a camouflage uniform, and that's all that I saw. All of them wore those uniforms. And when I was beaten right in front of the cell, some of them asked that I be thrown into the dorm to scrub their floor, to clean their dorm; however, I wasn't taken into the dorm. I, as I was beaten, I fell down, and later on they stopped and they put me into the cell on the floor and they closed the door. After that, I wasn't taken into the dorm to clean it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems one of the marks of the military police in the former Yugoslavia, in the units that followed, is a white belt. Did they have a white belt or they didn't have a white belt? And you can answer if you agree with the first proposition with me. If it's something else, then please state so?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they didn't have white belts. Dragan Saponja did not have a white belt, he had a dark belt. And as far as I can remember, others didn't -- that I could see -- and those who beat me in front of the cell, I don't recall that I saw them wearing white belts. However, I listened to some of their conversations during the night because I couldn't sleep and they were on guard, so I listened to some of the conversations on the actions that they undertook, and based on that conversation, I concluded that they were the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we play the tape that we played earlier, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please roll the tape forward and identify the segment of the tape when Mr. Semenovic is being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the wrong way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is a Prosecutor's Exhibit, so -- could you roll it back there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, can you help? Where are we going to find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If my recollection serves me, it's at about 8 minutes on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Are we getting the tape rolled back or what is the status of the medium?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To be more precise, Your Honour, looking at my notes, it would be eight minutes 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please play the tape and the sound also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is page 8 of the transcript; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you roll it back until the Court gets the proper reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, down the page it starts, and the witness is referred to in the transcript as "Man" because his name is not repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we play it, I see the -- our own transcript refers to page 8. I said page 4. Presumably it's the passage beginning "Journalist on/off camera, we've heard that you're one of the rare inhabitants of this reception centre who came to Omarska on his own? Man: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the "Man" is Mr. Semenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you play the tape, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We heard that you're one of the rare inhabitants of this reception centre that came to Omarska on his own. Yes, that's correct. Can you explain why you did that? Why did you come here? I came here after waiting for a while and hiding here. I waited for all the prime actors in these horrendous events to be captured and for the truth to be established about the people who have done all this evil acts, so that my efforts and work as well as the statements I can give can be appreciated. Who do you have in mind? Who is responsible for all these horrors that took place here? First of all I have in mind the leader of the party for Bosnia and Krajina, Mirsad Mujadzic and Mirsad Mujadzic chairman of the party branch in Prijedor and also member of the party executive council for Bosnia and Herzegovina, also the persons who within the party organised all these military activities. Are your colleagues who are here with you, are they aware of your opinion? Are you able to state your opinion publicly why all this took place? I have spoken on two occasions about this, also in an interview for TV Krajina, I have made my statement, and I have sent a message to the people with respect to this situation that I am now personally witnessing in Bosnia, Krajina, and Prijedor, not theoretically like those who are watching from the denizens and who are the master minds behind all these. I don't know if you are aware of the fact that there are some foreign reporters who came here, and the reason why they came here is because in the past few days, the international media have stated that in the Republic of Srpska, so in this territory here there are concentration camps for Muslims and Croats. Since you have stated that you have come here on your own free will, can you tell us whether this is a concentration camp or this is a reception centre? What can you tell them? I would like to tell them that the military operations caused such consequences that it was necessary for the people to group up both for their own safety and for the survival, and this centre does not have the characteristics of the concentration camp in the sense that is stated by the political propaganda. And one last question: Before the war broke out here, were the Muslims in any way preparing themselves for the war? In the past few months --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: We can stop the tape here, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, you have testified yesterday that you were given a statement to read before this interview. I am just asking you: Did you have that statement in front of you when you made this interview?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. When the journalist from Prijedor arrived, Mr. Ecim, he brought a statement which I was to read and he was going to tape it with a camera. And then later on, he wanted me to interpret this statement without a statement. He taped me twice. And following that, this interview took place when the Serbian SRNA television outlet taped this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't have that statement in front of you when SRNA took this statement?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Ecim offer for you to speak to the foreign journalists?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when the foreign journalists came in to visit the centre Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A day after the interview conducted by Zivko Ecim, it was I believe one day later that the four journalists arrived and then the police took me from the glass house and took me upstairs and up there there were the crews of the international TV media, and they refused to take me, and then they took me to a room on the first floor when this interview then took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple of minor points, Your Honours. Mr. Semenovic, have you been a member of the Territorial Defence in Trnopolje after you finished your regular military service? To what duty were you assigned as a reservist?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Territorial Defence. I put myself at this position on the eve of the war when the TO needed to be expanded because there were no other ways to legally organise defence, and before the war, after completing my regular military service, I was part of the reserve forces, reserve units, which every couple of years would be called up for military exercises, that was the only duty. Some were called every two or three years, some were called every seven or eight years. Within ten years, I was only called up once, and I believe that was sometime in 1984 or '85, I am not entirely sure. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After signing up for the Territorial Defence, have you at any time received a weapon from anyone?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not, no, because there weren't weapons to be had, and those weapons that were around, it was supposed to be taken only by the persons who were on the front-lines. So if they were to be killed, the others would take over from them and keep defending Kozarac and their villages. The majority of people who reported to these reserve -- these units did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just testified that you were in the reserve composition of the Yugoslav Army after you finished your regular service. In the time of emergency, at a time of mobilisation, you had your place where to report. Where was that place supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In law, that place was called gathering point. When we had that military exercise in 1984 or '85, we received calls, and those who received them had to report to this gathering point, and this gathering point where I was supposed to report was in the area of Orlovci, that is the Upper Orlovci, at the intersection off to the right, there is a local road, and down that road somewhere, a couple of kilometres down that road, that is where the gathering point or the meeting point was. When everybody reported there, from there, everybody would go to the location where the military exercise then took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Gornji Orlovci remained your Zborno Mesto for the rest of your reserve service; right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. This meeting point or gathering point, also called Zborno Mesto was a point where everybody who was to take part in this military exercise was meeting or gathering. From there, from that point, we all travelled to the location where the actual military exercise was then to take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm directing your attention now to the beginning of September of 1991. Have you received a summons as a military reservist and at that time still under the jurisdiction of JNA to report to active duty?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had the jurisdiction? What body had jurisdiction to issue the summons for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that it was the secretariat for the People's Defence which issued this call, I believe it was this secretariat, but I'm not entirely sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it fair to state that Mr. Becir Medunjanin from Kozarac was Nacelnik, meaning head of that body?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that he was. I am not sure, but I believe that he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was very close friend of yours or close political associate of yours, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, a political associate. That, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether men of your age at that time were called up for service, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, many were called up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've been through this call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Anything else for the witness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, you retracted the statement that you've given to SRNA television, of course. But when was the first time that you retracted that statement?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not understand the word "Retracted."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would say "disavowed" or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "Contradicted."

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You said yesterday that what you reported as saying on television, you, in fact, didn't mean. You explained that. And what counsel is asking, if you can answer, is when, for the first time, did you take that statement back? Can you assist?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that for the first time when I managed to leave the area of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in conversation with the official bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is what I stated to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is indeed a very important statement in the life of any man who has suffered as much as you did. I'm just trying to see whether you recall who was that official that you stated to and when?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During the conversation which I had about my stay in the camp, I believe that this conversation was conducted with one of the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, it was the first time then that I talked about these events and that is when I spoke about it, about this interview and about the taping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could remember, perhaps the month or a season and what year that you spoke to representatives of the Tribunal and that you took back this statement?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In 1995, I believe in late '95, but I'm not sure. It could have even been early '96.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left the territory of Krajina on January 15, 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On 15th or 19th, I am not sure, but within that time period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any approval of Mr. Kupresanin to leave the Serbian-held territory because that point is not completely clear to us? If you could just state what conversation have you had with Mr. Kupresanin directly or indirectly before you were permitted to leave?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Regarding my departure, I never talked to Kupresanin. A representative of the International Red Cross talked to Mr. Kupresanin and a gentleman called Nikola Granic, he was director of the Plon company in Banja Luka who had good personal relations with Kupresanin and a dentist called Emir. So they talked to him and he gave approval for me to leave this territory, and they were engaged in some activities there of which I did not know. Later on, when this dentist named Emir came to me and asked me to sign a statement in which I'm expressing my gratitude to Mr. Kupresanin for having saved my life which was to stay in Banja Luka, in return, through auspices of the IRC, they were going to enable me to go to Norway. I do not know why Norway, but they said that they could do that and I would be able to leave for Norway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you do know, what is the ethnic background on Mr. Nikola Granic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not sure. I believe he is a Croat, but I'm not entirely certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So isn't it fair to conclude that even in '93, that Mr. Kupresanin had a close relationship with a Muslim doctor and Croat in Banja Luka, and all three of them, a Serb, a Muslim, and a Croat assisted you to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And Mr. Bernard Schwitzer, or Schwartzer, a representative of the International Red Cross. But I know that the three gentlemen were all close friends, they were all wartime orphans from World War II, and all three of them grew up in a house, in a Muslim household. I believe it was the mother of this dentist, I believe that she raised them, and so they continued this friendship, continued into 1993. Following that, Mr. Granic had to leave Banja Luka. I believe that he went through to Slovenia. That is as far as I heard, and I do not know what happened to Mr. Emir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is indeed very interesting and very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may be, but I wonder if you can assist us --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Semenovic, and, Your Honour, if I can just have a minute to consult with co-counsel, whether we have any more questions? Thank you, Your Honours. We don't have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do have some brief re-examination, but in light of the long discussion about the camp and the position, relative position of things, we had a diagram prepared over the lunch, but I haven't had an opportunity to show it to the Defence. I wonder if we might take the break early in order to do that, and some film that would also help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I hope this can be dealt with fairly rapidly so we can make a start with another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I can add this while you're on your feet, Mr. Keegan. The Trial Chamber have been considering arrangements for Friday. We don't intend sitting late at all that day. There are other matters we have to attend to. And, in fact, we have in mind finishing at 1.00 p.m. and starting at 9.00, slightly earlier than usual. I don't imagine that is going to cause anybody any inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, we appear to have lost nearly ten minutes during that break. That was no fault of yours, of course, but we will sit on till ten past five to make up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour Re-examined by Mr. Keegan:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, with respect to the issue or the questions regarding the order of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence forces on about April 8th, as you testified, earlier you had testified as to your knowledge about attacks on Muslim areas in eastern Bosnia, including Zvornik and Bijeljina and others. Are you aware, did those attacks come before or after this issuance of the formation of the Territorial Defence for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It came before the order on the establishment of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this photo marked, shown to the witness, and then put on the ELMO, please. I apologise, Your Honour, we got it quickly during the break and we only have one available. It can be produced to others. It was shown to the Defence during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photo is marked number 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you put it on the ELMO, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, I'm directing your attention to the uniform that that individual is wearing. Do you recognise what type of uniform that is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is the uniform of the special police, the one that I have mentioned several times and explained. It was a camouflage uniform but with -- in purple hues, so it's darker than the regular camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could that photograph be given to the Judges, please, so they can actually see the colours? Next, Your Honour, we have a diagram of the -- a diagram to present to the witness, a copy has already been provided to the Defence during the break. This would be Exhibit 45, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, do you recognise that diagram, please, what that represents?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It represents Trnopolje and, in the middle of the drawing are the sketches of the local commune and the school buildings and then there's a soccer field --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, if we could put that on the overhead, then you can describe it so everyone can see what you are pointing to on the screen, please. Could that be panned back just a bit, please? Thank you. That's good. First question, Mr. Semenovic: Do you recognise the roads that are depicted there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is the road, Trnopolje-Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please put a "K" on that diagram, write a "K" at the end of the road in the direction of Kozarac, please?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the other road that is depicted, it runs basically left to right as it is now existing on that diagram and on the computer screens.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the road Trnopolje-Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you put a "P" on the diagram at the end of the road in the direction of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Indicates)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that road were to continue to the left, to what area in the municipality would it go?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It would continue towards Omarska, not towards the municipality but towards Omarska, and that is the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you put an "O" there then, please?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Indicates)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I could direct your attention to the buildings that you had begun to describe when you first received the diagram, you referred to the building of the local commune or Mjesna Zajednica. Could you please point that out?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This complex of structures is the local commune. This structure here is the old cinema theatre, and in the middle were the offices of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Semenovic, put a "T" next to the building which contained the theatre, as you described, or the cinema, excuse me, put a "T" next to that building?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Indicates)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned in your -- I'm sorry. Could you also then describe the next building to the right of the Mjesna Zajednica complex. Could you please describe what that is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the building of the elementary school, and here it is on the drawing. This is the part where the classrooms were, and this farther part is the sports hall that was part of the school complex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please put an "S" next to the school building?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Indicates)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could please pan back from that in the audio booth? Thank you. Now, Mr. Semenovic, could you please give, on the diagram, a general indication of the area from which you entered the camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this area (indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please put an "A" in that area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Indicates)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point, Your Honour, we also have a video, it was a video provided to the Defence on 3 July. I believe it shows the areas that the Defence was interested in this morning in a much more clear resolution, as well as the area behind the local commune building and the school area, as the witness has described. If we could run that tape, please? That would be Exhibit 46, Your Honour, the tape. If we could hold the film there for a minute, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, do you recognise the area that has just been shown on this segment of the video?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the building where the storage house of the agricultural co-op was, and the thing next to the wire fence was the yard belonging to the co-op.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could advance the film, please? Continue the film? (Videotape played) What road would that be shot from? Where would the cameraman be standing, Mr. Semenovic, on which of the two roads?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the road Trnopolje-Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I apologise. I meant the prior scene? That shot there.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The camera man is on the intersection of the Trnopolje-Kozarac and Trnopolje-Prijedor roads, and the electrical power substation is to the left of the image.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if you could advance the film, please? (Videotape played) Hold the film there, please? Now, from this shot, Mr. Semenovic, can you recognise where the camera man would be standing?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The camera man is on the road, the Trnopolje-Kozarac near the place which I described before, maybe 30 metres farther down, and behind the wire fence and the people there is the building where the cinema theatre was, and next to it we see the local commune building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Advance the film, please. Advance the film, please. (Videotape played) If you could hold the film right there? Mr. Semenovic, can you recognise the uniform that the man on the right, far right, on the other side of the fence, is wearing?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The man on the right has the uniform of the special police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could advance the film, please? (Videotape played) And if you could turn up the volume, please? Never mind then. Just fast-forward the tape, please, to the next section. (Videotape played) That's sufficient, thank you. If you would advance the film? Stop. Thank you. If you hold the film right there, please? Mr. Semenovic, can you tell from that shot what area the camera man is now standing in?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think the camera man is at the beginning of the road, Trnopolje-Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could back the film up slightly, please? Right there is good. What is the building that we're looking at there, Mr. Semenovic, in the picture, that's the large building and it takes up most of the picture?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's the building of the old cinema.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building then that you see to the far right in front of the cinema with the orange roof, which building would that be?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's one of the houses that are across from the local commune building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could advance the film, please? (Videotape played) You can fast-forward it. And if you could now hold the film, please? Thank you. Back it up slightly and then just play at normal speed. Back it up, please? (Videotape played) Now play at normal speed. Thank you. You may advance it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, do you recognise this field area with the woods behind it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this is the area behind the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You may stop the film. Your Honour, we would offer the entirety of the tape. We will provide -- we pulled it together rather quickly, but we will provide a complete transcript in addition to the number of interviews that are conducted in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, one final question: When Mr. Kupresanin came to take you from the camp and then all of the events that transpired, which you've already discussed, did he come to take you out of the camp before or after the international press had visited Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The following morning after the foreign journalists and international representatives came to visit the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, thank you for coming. You are released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't know if there were any further questions. We would like to make him subject to recall, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I hope it will be only be for a very good reason indeed. He's been here for the better part of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: We object to that, Your Honour. Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think you can object, but, Mr. Semenovic, I hope that you will not have to come back because you have given evidence for long enough, but subject to that, you are released. Thank you for coming. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The next witness, Your Honour, would be Mr. Edward Vulliamy, it's V-U-L-L-I-A-M-Y.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just approach the registrar for 30 seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You may be seated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Keegan:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please state for the record your full name?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Edward Sebastian Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you're a citizen of the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend university, and what were your major areas of studies?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I was educated at Oxford University in the United Kingdom where I studied philosophy with politics and briefly at the University of Florence in Italy, again studying philosophy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after completing your studies, did you become a journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What organisation do you currently work for?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I work for the Guardian newspaper in the United Kingdom and for its sister paper, The Observer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What areas of interest do you generally cover?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I've been covering a number of things over the past 15 years. Conflicts in various parts of the world for both my newspaper and a television company before that and during the past six years or so, overwhelmingly the wars in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what particular awards have you received as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Before Yugoslavia, I won an award called the Royal Television Society Award for Current Affairs that was for a film unconnected with Yugoslavia. Since covering the wars, I have won the British Press Award International Reporter of the Year, '92. The same year I won, I think, the Foreign Correspondent of the Year awarded by a program called "What The Papers Say." I won Amnesty International Award for Journalism in '93, I won a thing called the James Cameron award in '94, which is referred to as the British Pulitzer award, and then last year I won the British Press Award's International Reporter of the Year, again for a retrospective history of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when did you first begin to cover the break-up of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I first went to the former Yugoslavia, professionally that is, in the summer of 1991, June 1991, initially to cover the conflict that had -- that was breaking out in what was then the west of Yugoslavia in Slovenia, the first shots of the war, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could have the map provided to the witness, please? I want the witness to put it on the ELMO, please. A copy of this map has already been provided to the Defence, Your Honour. The purpose of this particular map is because it lists the towns within the former Yugoslavia, many of them important towns, without any other sort of interference, the topographical kinds of marks or roads that can distract from where the towns are.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map is marked Exhibit 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could have the overhead turned on, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, if you could, you indicated that you first began your coverage in Slovenia. Can you briefly describe the areas you covered there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid we start off slightly off this map, off the top left-hand corner, you can see Slovenia sort of peeping in here. I was in this area here, in the Slovenia capital of Ljubljana, which is about here, off the map, and in this area in the east of Slovenia adjacent to Croatia. That was the first phase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from there, where did you next go in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, a fresh phase of the war began in Croatia, and I was assigned to move with it, and I worked for the next few months in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could indicate that area on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in Zagreb, the capital, obviously, in what was a frontline between the emergent Croatian forces and the then Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, firstly around this area, Sisak, Petrinja, Glina; down here, Slunj; and this area on the edge of what was called the Krajina where the Croatian populations and Serbian populations met. I worked for the most part in this area here, in the east of Croatia and the west of what is now Serbia, on the Croatian side, in the town of Osijek, which was under siege by the JNA, in Vukovar, right here on the border, also under siege by the JNA. I was in Vukovar until I think the penultimate day when you could be. Came out through a road cut through the cornfields. Thereafter covered the siege of Vukovar from a town called Vinkovci, which is here, and a little village called Mustar (phoen), which is not marked; and during this period, I was also working on the JNA side with the Yugoslav People's Army, which was in the process of becoming the Serbian army, at a place called Bogojevo, which is not marked. It's here somewhere; a garrison town. At this place, which was an important town called Sid, and in all this area here, Sombor, indeed, and you could go through Hungary to skirt the frontlines there. Then the third area in Croatia I worked during 1991 was down here on the coast, most particularly Dubrovnik which was under siege as well, and in the towns of Sibenik, further up the coast, and Zadar, further up again, which were also under shell fire and attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could move back to the area in eastern Croatia, around Vukovar, Vinkovci. Can you describe the type of forces that were engaged on both sides of the conflict and the type of weaponry which they had arrayed there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this questioning. It is outside the Prijedor area, outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Keegan, that prima facie seems a reasonable objection. What is your answer to this? What's the relevance of it, interesting though it is, about what the witness has to say? How is it going to assist us to try this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The description of the conflict here, Your Honour, will go to help establish the plan and pattern which you see later emerge within the Autonomous Region of Krajina and which is employed, in fact, in the Prijedor area and the municipalities surrounding it. Of course, keeping in mind the nature of the elements we have to prove for certain of the charges, the legal elements, we believe it is relevant. We will try and keep it brief, but we believe its relevance will be indicated as we get into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, we shan't stop you adducing this evidence. We accept your point about the width of the charges which you have to prove. But at the same time we shall encourage you to limit the evidence until we come to what is directly relevant here, and that's events in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, could you please describe the way that the forces were structured on both sides and the type of weaponry which were employed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. And I note the request for brevity. The Croatian army was a nascent army, a mixture of police, former soldiers, civilians, initially scantily armed, and a hodge-podge really of former regular soldiers and various militias which were formed often locally. On the other side, on the JNA side, you had a regular army, the Yugoslav People's Army, with the armaments at its disposal which were apparently considerable, as far as one could see. Acting as a director of and support echelon of irregulars who were fighting out in the villages that I worked in, on the Yugoslav/Serbian side. So you had an entwinement, really of an irregular army with irregulars with whom I spent a great deal of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to discern a pattern in the manner in which the attacks were conducted during the time you spent in this area on the Serbian side with the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object, and I want to thank you for giving me an opportunity to speak yesterday. My name is John Ostojic, and we object to both the form and foundation of the question asked by Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have just ruled it admissible. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The pattern was roughly as follows. Bogojevo, which is here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't believe the video monitor is on. I'm sorry, it is.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Bogojevo, which is roughly here, and Sid roughly there were essentially garrison towns where the armies would be based, where the echelons would be based, artillery and tanks and transport vehicles repaired, troops billeted. Sid would then feed the frontline, siege lines, for Vukovar and the artillery lines and water lines and tank lines around Vukovar, and Bogojevo would be similar deployed with regards to Osijek, and so the operation was astride the border, if you like, with the main bases and garrisons on the Serbian side and the fighting over on the Croatian side. I recall one particular night in a place called Bijelo Brdo, which is about here, where you could see it was fairly obviously arraigned, I was actually on the edge of a field across which the fighting was taking place. At the very frontline you had the irregulars with their machine guns, behind them were rows of tanks, and so the small arms fire would be between the irregulars across the field with the Croatians, the tanks and the actual shelling of Osijek, as it was in that case, was coming from directly behind them, a matter of 500 yards behind them, and then the logistics would all be taking place over the border back in Serbia. Given that you want me to be brief, I shan't go over it all again, but the same thing was happening in Sid over here regarding the siege of Vukovar, so you had this entwinement between regular and irregular forces with the officers, in particular a Colonel Uzelac I got to know quite well, making it plain that they were in charge of both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have, during the time you spent there, discussions with these irregular forces as to what their role and purpose in the conflict was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At length, yes, because we used to hang around with them in the cafes and so on and got to know what their aims were, which were the establishment of Serbian-only territory within Croatia, and indeed also, I must say, about their fears and the unpleasant experiences they had had in the nascent Croatia, a lot of them lost their jobs and so on, so they explained not only what they were fighting for, but why they were doing it. We spent a lot of time with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they see as their purpose with respect to the non-Serb population in those areas?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, they wanted to push them back as far as possible. They wanted to take Osijek, they wanted to push the Croats back as far as Zagreb, and if you allow me to be anecdotal, a chap once went "Zagreb, vroom" -- yes, that's the vernacular, I apologise. They wanted to take Osijek and push the Croats back as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you later moved on in the war, did you come across a very similar type of scenario in 1992 between the areas of Serbia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. There was a -- this was -- this would be the beginning of August 1992, so a different year, different war. And this was a place called Loznica, let's see if I can find it -- it's here. Just inside Serbia, on the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I went down there because we were looking at places where deportees, refugees, and alleged prisoners were being kept. Loznica was one of the camps where Bosnian Muslims who had been deported from this area were being kept within Serbia. That's another matter. But if I understand the question, and the point is that Loznica was once again a garrison town. You could see equipment being maintained, a lot of traffic across the border into this little place that I went to called Zepak from whence the deportees had come, and there was actually so much military movement going forward to furnish the troops here that we were able to cross the border ourselves without even being asked to show any papers; the border didn't really exist. The only difference really was that whereas in the first war there was actual fighting going on, because the Croats had armies which were indeed intimidating some of those who were fighting, very considerably, and indeed advancing at some points, here there was no actual fighting so much as simply occupation, deportation of civilians. So that was the difference, but the pattern was the same: garrison town and the military action, as it were, astride the border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the nature, the composition of the forces which you saw in that area crossing from Loznica into eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, what was the composition of the types of forces that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
